source.title: Going Beyond Neural Network Feature Similarity: The Network Feature Complexity and Its Interpretation Using Category Theory
source.authors: Yiting Chen; Zhanpeng Zhou; Jun-Chi Yan

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives a theoretical result connecting linear mode connectivity after permutation to functionally equivalent features in different networks, bearing on cross-seed feature convergence and representation interchangeability. Its empirical experiments mainly measure redundancy within individual networks, not convergence across models.
record.gate_note: The empirical results on feature distances, merging and pruning concern functionally equivalent features within a single network; they do not measure cross-model alignment, cross-modal alignment, recurring features across models, or dependence of alignment on similarity metrics or inputs. The paper's proposition about LMC is a theoretical result; empirical LMC results mentioned in the paper are cited from prior work and are not counted as rows.
record.test_reason: The only cross-network content is Proposition 3.2. It is a conditional theoretical argument: if two same-structure networks are linearly mode-connected after a permutation, their features are functionally equivalent. The paper never measures whether its own independently trained networks satisfy LMC or share features. It relies on cited prior work (Entezari, Ainsworth, Liu) for that. All empirical results concern redundancy among features within a single network (weight distances, self-permutation interpolation, IFM merging), which is a different construct from cross-model convergence. So no version is tested by the study's own results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusions concern within-network feature complexity: functionally equivalent features are widespread within a network and can be merged by IFM without fine-tuning. Larger networks learn more redundant features. Same-structure networks with higher feature complexity (ResNet50 v2) perform better. Complexity first rises then falls across layers. Equivalent-feature groups may correspond to specific semantics. The claim that LMC implies functional equivalence across networks is stated as a theoretical contribution, not an empirical finding.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a category-theoretic definition and weight-matching-based feature merging, rather than measuring representational similarity between independently trained networks using the original sources' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The IFM hyperparameter β changes how many features are merged and consequently testing accuracy. The paper also reports different accuracy decline under merging for ResNet50 v1 and v2.

fits_no_version.finding: Trained CNNs contain many near-duplicate (functionally equivalent) features within a layer. These can be merged without fine-tuning at limited accuracy cost, and the amount merged is larger for larger networks and easier tasks (CIFAR10 vs ImageNet). Within-layer feature complexity rises then falls with depth (Fig. 5a). Groups of equivalent features map to shared visual parts (Fig. 5b, 7, 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual trained vision networks learn redundant, functionally equivalent features within layers. The amount of redundancy grows with width and depth and shrinks with task difficulty and better training recipes.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says source code will be made publicly available)
record.problems: The empirical experiments are limited to image classification and do not test cross-model representational alignment, cross-modal alignment, or convergence across seeds. The LMC connection is conditional and theoretical; the paper cites prior empirical LMC findings rather than testing LMC between its own model pairs. Several reported compression outcomes are qualitative or figure-based, and uncertainty estimates are not given for the main accuracy results.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported result was included because the remaining experiments concern pruning-method comparisons, layerwise feature complexity, or semantic visualizations within individual networks, rather than the claim's convergence versions.

untested.parts: No cross-model alignment as a function of scale or capability. The 'larger networks learn more redundant features' finding is within-network.
No models trained from different seeds are compared. Whether they satisfy LMC or share features is assumed from cited work, not measured.
No mapping, stitching or permutation alignment between two distinct trained networks is performed or evaluated.
Guided-backprop semantics of equivalent-feature groups are shown within one VGG16 only, not across models.
No comparison of similarity metrics or inputs for cross-model convergence. The authors only argue in prose that similarity measures are 'vague'.
No measurement of the degree or causes of cross-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and its V3/V4 'supports' labels rest solely on a conditional theorem whose premise is imported from cited empirical work. That is not the study's own result bearing on whether the versions hold, so the labels are removed. The paper motivates itself by questioning feature-similarity measures, which touches V6 in prose only. The abstract says 'low-level semantic' while the body says 'high-level semantic'.

versions.untested_parts: Whether representations of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives and data become more aligned with scale and capability.
Cross-modal alignment of paired images and captions as vision and language models improve.

The paper gives a conditional theoretical result for same-structure networks satisfying LMC after permutation, but does not empirically test independently initialized seeds, how often they satisfy LMC, or how many shared features or subspaces they learn.
The result concerns permutation correspondence under LMC; it does not test stitching, relative representations, unpaired-data mappings, or other linear mappings empirically.
Whether the same interpretable features or circuits recur across different models.
Whether measured cross-model convergence changes with similarity metric settings or input data, including out-of-distribution inputs.
Whether cross-model alignment is incomplete or plateaus, or is explained by shared training data or objectives.

rows.subject: Two same-structure networks with parameters θa and θb satisfying LMC after permutation
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical proposition: derives a natural isomorphism between the networks' feature mappings from LMC after permutation.
rows.measure: Existence of natural isomorphism / functionally equivalent features
rows.value: The paper states that a permutation under which the networks satisfy LMC implies a natural isomorphism and functionally equivalent features.
rows.note: Conditional theoretical result, not an empirical measurement of independently trained models. It establishes a permutation correspondence under the stated LMC condition.
rows.check: Not a result row. It is a conditional theoretical proposition with no measurement of any model pair. The premise (LMC after permutation) is taken from cited work, not tested here. The proof also leans on the LLFC equation (Eq. 12) rather than LMC alone. It cannot show whether seeds converge (V3) or whether representations map with little loss (V4).

source_check.correct: Retain as a conditional theoretical proposition rather than an empirical result row.
source_check.problem: The proposition is accurately described, but no independently trained model pair is measured.

rows.subject: VGG16
rows.stage_stated: trained on CIFAR10 for 150 epochs with SGD
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized weight-matching distances among features in the last convolution layer.
rows.measure: Minimum normalized weight distance between two features
rows.note: This is a within-network feature-distance result, not a comparison between independently trained networks.
rows.check: Within-network weight distances only. The value 2e-15 is a single minimum pair, not a typical distance.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for representation convergence; 2e−15 is the minimum within-network feature distance and is explicitly stated in the text.
source_check.problem: Within-network distances cannot establish any listed cross-model claim; the figure_only designation also overlooks the textual value.

rows.subject: VGG16
rows.operation_detail: Interpolated model parameters between the model and a version with matched equivalent features permuted; compared with random permutations of the same number of features.
rows.baseline: Random permutation of the same number of features is shown as a comparator; original accuracy is not stated here.
rows.value: Figure only; the text says interpolation between equivalent-feature permutations hardly affects performance.
rows.note: The comparison is between permutations of one network, not between independently trained models.
rows.check: Interpolation is between a network and a permutation of itself, not between independently trained networks.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for representation convergence; interpolation between one network and its equivalent-feature permutation hardly affects performance.
source_check.problem: The experiment compares permutations of one network and cannot establish convergence across independently trained models.

rows.subject: VGG16
rows.operation_detail: Applied Iterative Feature Merging (IFM) to merge features and reduce parameters without fine-tuning.

conditions.value: not stated for this reported point

rows.measure: Test accuracy at the reported remaining-parameter fraction
rows.value: 91.78% at 23.03% of the original number of parameters
rows.note: The authors describe the resulting accuracy as relatively close to the original; this is within-network compressibility, not cross-model convergence.
rows.check: The state is relative to the study's own within-network redundancy finding: 91.78% vs 93.51% at 23.03% of parameters. It bears on no version.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for representation convergence; VGG16 retains 23.03% of parameters with 91.78% accuracy versus 93.51% originally.
source_check.problem: The reported compression result is accurate, but within-network compressibility cannot establish a listed convergence version.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Applied IFM to merge features and reduce parameters without fine-tuning.
rows.baseline: Original testing accuracy not stated for this result.
rows.value: The paper says up to 60% of parameters could be reduced without significantly affecting testing accuracy.
rows.note: Qualitative statement about within-network redundancy; no specific accuracy or compression point is given.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for representation convergence; up to 60% of ResNet18 parameters can be removed without significantly affecting testing accuracy.
source_check.problem: The compression percentage does not measure partial cross-model convergence.

rows.subject: VGG networks
rows.size_stated: VGG11, VGG13, VGG16 and VGG19 are named in the relevant figures; individual sizes not stated
rows.operation_detail: Applied IFM to merge features and measured parameter reduction and top-1 accuracy.

conditions.value: VGG networks; results described in aggregate

rows.note: The paper reports the approximate result in aggregate and says larger networks permit more equivalent features to be merged.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for representation convergence; IFM removes approximately 5% of VGG parameters on ImageNet.
source_check.problem: The parameter reduction measures within-network redundancy, not partial cross-model convergence.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Applied IFM to merge features and measured parameter reduction and top-1 accuracy.
rows.note: Approximate result for ResNet50; the paper also reports different accuracy responses for the two checkpoints in R8.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for representation convergence; IFM removes approximately 10% of ResNet50 parameters on ImageNet.
source_check.problem: The parameter reduction measures within-network redundancy, not partial cross-model convergence.

rows.subject: ResNet50 v2
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy decline under IFM with ResNet50 v1 as features were merged.
rows.measure: Top-1 accuracy decline as features are merged
rows.baseline: ResNet50 v1 is the stated comparator; its baseline accuracy is 76.13%, while v2 baseline accuracy is 80.86%.
rows.value: The paper states that v2 accuracy decreases faster than v1 accuracy as more features are merged.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as v2 learning more diverse features; this is a within-network compression comparison, not a cross-model alignment result.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for representation convergence; ResNet50 v2 accuracy decreases faster under merging than v1; original top-1 accuracies are 80.86% and 76.13%, respectively.
source_check.problem: Different compression responses across checkpoints do not measure alignment or partial convergence between their representations.

relation.reason: The paper discusses cross-network equivalence and offers a conditional theoretical interpretation, without measuring convergence between independently trained networks.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure within-network feature redundancy. Proposition 3.2 is conditional on cross-network connectivity, whose occurrence is attributed to cited studies rather than tested here.

source_check.notes: Appendix B.1 invokes the LLFC equation in proving the proposition stated using LMC; the proof therefore relies on an additional connectivity property. The supplied text identifies itself as a preprint under review and does not substantiate the pack's ICLR 2023 reviewed designation.

reader_labels.reason: The paper's Proposition 3.2 states that this condition implies functionally equivalent features; this is a conditional theoretical result, not an empirical test of seed convergence (R1).
